clue.text: Madeleine reminded him

parts.note: the little cake dipped in tea that sets off a flood of memory in the opening volume of In Search of Lost Time, so its author is the man it reminded

explanation.surface: A woman named Madeleine jogged some man's memory.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Madeleine' looks like a woman's name, but it is the small French sponge cake whose taste brings back the narrator's childhood in the famous scene of the French novel.
explanation.definitionFit: The French novelist made the madeleine the trigger of involuntary memory in his great novel.

clue.text: English recorder of French lives with German car

parts.note: mit is the German word for with
a Ford is a make of car

explanation.surface: An English biographer of French figures drives a German car.
explanation.walkthrough: Nancy Mitford wrote lives of Madame de Pompadour, Voltaire and Louis XIV, hence 'recorder of French lives'.
explanation.definitionFit: Nancy Mitford, an English writer, published biographies of French historical figures such as Madame de Pompadour and Voltaire.

clue.text: Chaucerian tale-teller as gothic novelist

definitions.meaning: one of the Canterbury pilgrims, the estate manager who tells his own tale
Clara ..., author of The Old English Baron, an eighteenth-century gothic romance

explanation.surface: One of Chaucer's storytellers doubles as a writer of gothic fiction.
explanation.definitionFit: The estate steward among Chaucer's pilgrims tells a tale, and Clara of that surname wrote gothic fiction.

clue.text: Upwards with tall poet?

definitions.meaning: the Latin motto meaning ever higher
a tall poet is a long fellow, so this is the title of the famous poem by Longfellow

explanation.surface: Someone climbs higher in the company of a lofty versifier.
explanation.walkthrough: 'tall poet' is a pun: tall means long, so the poet is Longfellow, whose poem of that title has a youth climbing an Alpine pass with a banner.
explanation.definitionFit: The Latin word means 'higher', used as a motto of aspiration, and it titles Longfellow's poem of ambition.

clue.text: Little sparrow with no regrets

definitions.meaning: the French stage nickname, meaning little sparrow, of the Parisian chanteuse Edith Gassion
she sang the famous song declaring she regrets nothing

explanation.surface: A small bird feels no remorse.
explanation.definitionFit: Edith, the French singer nicknamed 'La Môme' sparrow, recorded 'Non, je ne regrette rien'.

clue.text: London venue's exhibition of Macedonian queen

definitions.meaning: the possessive of Olympia, the large exhibition hall in west London
the wife of Philip II and mother of Alexander the Great

explanation.surface: A London hall stages a show about an ancient queen.
explanation.walkthrough: Olympia is a big exhibition centre in Kensington, London, so 'exhibition' also suits the surface; the queen's name happens to be that venue's possessive.
explanation.definitionFit: The mother of Alexander the Great bore this name, which also spells the possessive of the London exhibition hall.

clue.text: French novelist of The Cobra's Return?

indicators.note: the title-like word Return says the serpent's name is read backwards

parts.note: a naga is a cobra, sacred serpent of Indian myth, so the cobra's is naga's

explanation.surface: A French novelist wrote a book called The Cobra's Return.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The Cobra's Return' looks like a book title; 'Return' reverses NAGAS to give the author of Bonjour Tristesse.
explanation.definitionFit: Françoise Sagan was the French author of Bonjour Tristesse.

clue.text: When I want to read a novel, I write one " he said

definitions.text: When I want to read a novel, I write one " he said

parts.words: When I want to read a novel, I write one " he said
parts.note: a famous quip by the Victorian prime minister who was also a novelist, author of Sybil and Coningsby

explanation.surface: An author explains that he writes the novels he wants to read.
explanation.walkthrough: The quotation is attributed to Benjamin Disraeli, the British prime minister who wrote novels.
explanation.definitionFit: The Victorian statesman and novelist is credited with this remark about writing fiction for his own reading.

clue.text: Mark's wife not so young, we're told

indicators.note: says the words are heard, so is-old is taken by its sound

parts.note: someone not so young is old, so she is old

explanation.surface: Someone reports that Mark's wife is getting on in years.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mark' is King Mark of Cornwall, whose wife falls in love with Tristan; 'we're told' turns 'is old' into her name by sound.
explanation.definitionFit: In the Tristan legend the Irish princess marries King Mark of Cornwall.

clue.text: New Troy cache reveals government like that of the Incas

definitions.text: government like that of the Incas

indicators.note: something new is a fresh form, so the letters of these two words are made into a new arrangement

explanation.surface: A newly found hoard at Troy reveals how the Incas were ruled.
explanation.walkthrough: 'New' rearranges TROY CACHE; the Inca emperor was held divine, so his rule was by a god's representative.
explanation.definitionFit: The Inca ruler was worshipped as a son of the sun, so the state was ruled by divine authority.

clue.text: Roman jurist happy in Paris and America

parts.note: gai is French for happy or merry
US is the abbreviation for the United States of America

explanation.surface: A Roman lawyer is content in both France and the States.
explanation.walkthrough: Gaius was a second-century Roman jurist whose Institutes survive.
explanation.definitionFit: The second-century legal writer whose Institutes became a key text of Roman law.

clue.text: A single sick playwright

parts.note: a single thing is one
sick means ill

explanation.surface: One playwright on his own is unwell.
explanation.walkthrough: Eugene O'Neill was the American dramatist of Long Day's Journey into Night.
explanation.definitionFit: Eugene O'Neill was a Nobel-winning American dramatist.

clue.text: Reds plan unusual architectural feature

indicators.note: unusual means out of the ordinary, so the letters of these two words are put in another order

explanation.surface: Communists draw up an odd design for a building.
explanation.walkthrough: 'unusual' rearranges REDS PLAN.
explanation.definitionFit: A curved triangular space between an arch and its frame is a familiar feature in buildings.

clue.text: Make sudden move, that is like Galsworthian rogue

parts.note: to dart is to move suddenly and quickly
i.e. is the abbreviation of id est, that is

explanation.surface: A rogue from Galsworthy makes a sudden lunge.
explanation.walkthrough: Montague Dartie is the spendthrift, philandering husband of Winifred Forsyte in Galsworthy's Forsyte Saga.
explanation.definitionFit: Montague Dartie is the disreputable gambler married into the Forsyte family in Galsworthy's novels.

clue.text: Aristotelian theme might be bombast

definitions.meaning: the art of persuasion, the subject of one of Aristotle's treatises
inflated, showy language

explanation.surface: A subject Aristotle wrote about might be just hot air.
explanation.definitionFit: Aristotle wrote a treatise on the art of persuasive speaking, and the word also means pompous, empty speech.

clue.text: Dancing girl in ballet

definitions.meaning: a Hindu temple dancer
the classical ballet by Petipa and Minkus set in India, about a temple dancer, which takes its title from her calling

explanation.surface: A girl dances in a ballet.
explanation.definitionFit: The French word for an Indian temple dancer titles the Petipa ballet about one.

clue.text: Reconciliation in one day by Al Alvarez

definitions.meaning: making amends, bringing estranged parties together
Day of ... is a 1991 novel by the critic and poet Al Alvarez

explanation.surface: Peace is made in a single day, courtesy of a writer.
explanation.walkthrough: The second definition is a title: Al Alvarez wrote the novel Day of Atonement, so this word belongs to his 'day'.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means making amends or reconciliation, and it completes the title of Alvarez's novel Day of ...

clue.text: He said that he wrote with Aunt Edna in mind

definitions.text: He said that he wrote with Aunt Edna in mind

parts.words: He said that he wrote with Aunt Edna in mind
parts.note: Aunt Edna was the imagined respectable middle-class theatregoer invented by the dramatist of The Browning Version

explanation.surface: A writer claims he always thought of his aunt as his audience.
explanation.walkthrough: Terence Rattigan coined 'Aunt Edna' as the typical playgoer he wrote for; 'Aunt Edna' looks like a real relative.
explanation.definitionFit: The English playwright Terence Rattigan said he wrote for the conservative theatregoer he named Aunt Edna.

clue.text: Kafkaesque work of Yonge?

definitions.meaning: the novel by Kafka about Josef K's prosecution
Charlotte M. Yonge also wrote a novel with that title, a sequel to The Daisy Chain

explanation.surface: A nightmarish piece of writing is ascribed to a Victorian novelist.
explanation.definitionFit: Kafka's novel of an incomprehensible prosecution shares its title with an 1864 novel by Charlotte Yonge.

clue.text: Burned (while topless), Marlowe reports

parts.note: Marlowe's Faustus says Helen's face burnt the topless structures of Ilium, the tall buildings of Troy

explanation.surface: Marlowe reports someone burned while going topless.
explanation.walkthrough: 'topless' suggests sunbathing, but Doctor Faustus has 'the face that launched a thousand ships, And burnt the topless towers of Ilium': topless means too high to see the top.
explanation.definitionFit: In Doctor Faustus, the high buildings of Troy are burned, described as topless.

clue.text: Wilde lord found by the sea in Sussex

definitions.meaning: Lord ... is the dandy hero of An Ideal Husband
...-by-Sea is a seaside place near Worthing

explanation.surface: A Wildean aristocrat turns up at the seaside in southern England.
explanation.walkthrough: Sussex is a county on England's south coast; Goring-by-Sea is a resort there.
explanation.definitionFit: Lord Goring is a character in Wilde's An Ideal Husband, and Goring-by-Sea is a Sussex coastal village.

clue.text: Example coming up about demand to students from novelist

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so one piece goes around the other
in a down clue, coming up means read from bottom to top, so backwards

parts.note: e.g. abbreviates for example
to demand is to ask
L is a learner, so two Ls are students

explanation.surface: A novelist's example rises around a demand put to students.
explanation.walkthrough: 'coming up' suits a down clue: the example abbreviation is read upwards. 'about' wraps that round the demand, and two learners (L, from L-plates) follow.
explanation.definitionFit: Elizabeth Gaskell wrote Cranford and North and South.

clue.text: "… Fancy's child, / Warble his natives — - — wild" (Milton)

definitions.text: "… Fancy's child, / Warble his natives — - — wild" (Milton)

parts.words: "… Fancy's child, / Warble his natives — - — wild" (Milton)
parts.note: a fill-in-the-blank from L'Allegro, where Shakespeare, Fancy's child, warbles his native songs untaught, the gap being a woodland call

explanation.surface: A line of Milton's verse with a word left blank.
explanation.walkthrough: Milton's L'Allegro reads 'Or sweetest Shakespeare, Fancy's child, / Warble his native wood-notes wild'; the clue prints the gap with dashes.
explanation.definitionFit: A natural, untutored song like a bird's in the forest; Milton uses it of Shakespeare's artless genius.

clue.text: His Lenten Stuffe was a red herring

definitions.text: His Lenten Stuffe was a red herring

parts.words: His Lenten Stuffe was a red herring
parts.note: the Elizabethan pamphleteer wrote Lenten Stuffe in praise of Great Yarmouth and its red herring

explanation.surface: Someone's food for Lent was a misleading distraction.
explanation.walkthrough: 'red herring' looks like a false lead, but Thomas Nashe's Lenten Stuffe (1599) literally praises the smoked fish of Yarmouth.
explanation.definitionFit: Thomas Nashe, the Elizabethan writer, wrote Lenten Stuffe, a mock encomium of the red herring.

clue.text: He was seen as inimitable, yet in the offing

definitions.meaning: The Inimitable ... is a Wodehouse collection named after the valet
... in the Offing is a Wodehouse novel about the same valet

explanation.surface: Someone thought matchless was still on the horizon.
explanation.definitionFit: Wodehouse's valet appears in the titles The Inimitable Jeeves and Jeeves in the Offing.

clue.text: Contents of The Old Curiosity Shop

definitions.text: Contents of The Old Curiosity Shop

parts.words: Contents of The Old Curiosity Shop
parts.note: not the Dickens novel's text but the stock of a curio shop: objets d'art, antiques and bric-a-brac

explanation.surface: This refers to what lies within Dickens's novel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The Old Curiosity Shop' suggests Dickens's novel; read literally, its contents are curios, objects of virtu.
explanation.definitionFit: A taste for curios or art objects, and collectively such objects, as stocked in a shop of curiosities.

clue.text: Heroic narrative, mostly from 6

indicators.note: mostly means all but a bit, so the last letter is dropped

parts.note: refers to the answer to 6 down, the French novelist

explanation.surface: An epic tale largely comes from another clue.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mostly' drops the final N from the answer to 6 down.
explanation.definitionFit: A long heroic story, originally an Old Norse prose epic.

clue.text: Macaulay derived pleasure from them

parts.note: Rose Macaulay wrote Pleasure of ... (1953), a study of decayed buildings

explanation.surface: Macaulay enjoyed something.
explanation.walkthrough: The Macaulay is not the historian but Rose Macaulay, whose Pleasure of Ruins surveys crumbling remains.
explanation.definitionFit: Rose Macaulay's book Pleasure of Ruins celebrates the remains of fallen buildings.

clue.text: Rosamond Lehmann's fruit-bearer from The Sea

definitions.text: Rosamond Lehmann's fruit-bearer from The Sea

parts.words: Rosamond Lehmann's fruit-bearer from The Sea
parts.note: Take Sea away from the title and the fruiting plant is left

explanation.surface: A novelist's fruit-bearing plant comes from the ocean.
explanation.walkthrough: Rosamond Lehmann wrote A Sea-Grape Tree (1976); the plant 'from The Sea' is the rest of that title.
explanation.definitionFit: A plant bearing grapes, named in the title of Lehmann's late novel.

clue.text: 1ac personage, sort of a lean Justine

indicators.note: sort of means a kind or version, so these letters are formed into another arrangement

explanation.surface: A character from Proust is something like a slim Justine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sort of' rearranges A LEAN JUSTINE; Jean Santeuil is the hero of Proust's early unfinished novel.
explanation.definitionFit: Jean Santeuil is the hero and title of the French novelist's posthumously published early novel.
